idiom_name: close(ch) + for range / v, ok receive
implementation_notes: Go replaces the sentinel value with channel state: close(ch) tells every receiver that no more values will be sent, for range drains the buffered values and then ends, and v, ok := <-ch reports closure directly. A single close stops all consumers of the channel, so the one-pill-per-consumer bookkeeping disappears; the price is sender-side discipline, because only a sender may close and only once. A sentinel value remains the better tool when a consumer must distinguish an orderly stop from other channel closures, or when the stop must travel through a channel that already carries data (for example a job carrying a Stop flag).
pitfalls: Sending on a closed channel - or closing twice - panics; only the sender closes, and only after all sends are done.
Closing is a broadcast: you cannot stop a single consumer of a shared channel this way.
Range over a nil channel blocks forever, and a channel that is never closed hangs every worker; pair the shutdown with a select on ctx.Done() when a deadline must bound it.
If producers can still race with close, the shutdown is itself a data race - coordinate the producers (WaitGroup) before closing.
